newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Japan, Korea, Thai stocks drop, quiet elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Korea, Thai stocks drop, quiet elsewhere.

text.p: Stock markets in Japan, South Korea and Thailand were pummeled on Thursday as a variety of factors peaked investor concerns about local economies.
Other markets were relatively quiet and some, such as Hong Kong, Australia and New Zealand, remained closed over the long Christmas holiday.
Stocks in Tokyo were jolted, among other things, by a percipitious drop in the yen against the U.S. dollar to more than 115, its lowest level in 44 months.
The key 225-share Nikkei average fell more than 700 points, or over three percent, to 18,819.92 before it clawed its way up slightly to close off 257.38 points, or 1.32 percent, at 19,291.58.
The fall brought the index below an important psychological benchmark of 19,000 for the first time in over a year.
The late improvement in the stock market mirrored a bounce in the yen, which drew support from comments by government officials.
A senior Bank of Japan official noted: "Regarding recent developments in the foreign exchang market, we are adequately and carefully monitoring the market," he said.
Traders said there was a general lack of confidence in the Japanese economy as well as in government policies designed to help the fragile economy.
"Gloom spread due to Japan's budget for fiscal 1997, which calls for a consumption tax hike," said Tadahiro Kamongwa, general manager at Yamaichi Securities in Tokyo.

The stock market also remains vulnerable to weakness in the financial sector, where institutions are still being hurt by a need to provide against losses from problem loans made during the "bubble" years.
In Seoul, stocks were hurt by labour unrest following the passage of a new labour law that allows for layoffs and more flexible work hours.
The composite index closed provisionally at 659.10, down 18.75 points, or 2.77 percent. A record 920 stocks fell, compared with only 64 stocks that rose.
The law was rammed through parliament Thursday morning and prompted the outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions to call a strike by its 550,000 memebers, crippling key export industries.
"I see a series of massive strikes in the first quarter of 1997," said Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Thai stocks shed 2.15 percent by midday amid disappointment over weaker than expected 1996 and 1997 economic data released by the central bank on Thursday.
The SET Index fell 18.11 points to 823.31 on thin baht turnover of 1.4 billion.
"Investors were not satisfied with some key economic data, including current account deficit and exports...," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.
Elsewhere in Asia, Malaysian stocks were off 3.13 points at 1,206.19, in light trading. Dealers attributed some of the declines to the drop in Tokyo.

Indonesian shares were last trading 2.33 points, or 0.37 percent, lower at 630.41 points in thin holiday trading, while in the Philippines, shares inched up 12.99 points, or 0.41 percent, at 3,165.52 by the close. Taiwan stocks ended a four-day winning streak to close off 46.69 points, or 0.67 percent, at 6,889.03 on profit-taking, while Singapore shares were higher by 9.44 points, or 0.43 percent, at 2,196.58.
